correctness.rationale: For uniform recursive-tree parent choices the non-root original fringe count satisfies EB_{N,k}=N/[k(k+1)] and fixed-k concentration. At Nq_N→lambda, independent edge marks yield independent Poisson intensities lambda/[k(k+1)]; the expected count of marked sizes>K is ≤Nq_N/(K+1). Two marked edges are ancestrally nested with expected count O(q_N²N log N)=o(1), so with high probability the actual non-root components coincide exactly with distinct uncut marked fringes. This proves ℓ¹ tightness in number of components, compound-Poisson root deficit W with jump probabilities 1/[k(k+1)], infinite E[W] for lambda>0, tail lambda/m, and ED_N~lambda log N for exact q_N=lambda/N. Binary reinforced-step conditioning supplies a uniform independent bit per percolated component, whose parity Fourier character is the indicator all components have even size. Odd N makes it identically zero; even N makes it asymptotically exp(-lambda sum_{k odd}1/[k(k+1)])=2^{-lambda}, hence TV 2^{-lambda-1}. Independently exhaustive n=2..6 parent-tree/edge-cut enumerations confirm both exact fringe means and parity character; they do not prove convergence.
residual_risks: Tree count tightness is ℓ¹ for component numbers, not uniform integrability of total mass; indeed E W=∞ at lambda>0.
The sharp heavy-tail coefficient invokes standard one-large-jump reasoning; no finite enumeration proves that asymptotic.

The classical random-recursive-tree fringe law is prior work, not novel by itself. Baur’s high-retention percolation theorems concern diverging cut counts, unlike this bounded-intensity regime. The joint marked-component spectrum and resulting exact parity mixing coefficient are not implied by the compared specific theorems. General Poisson thinning literature remains a genuine priority risk.
